New jet engines can produce 1,000 times less soot

In flight tests, a lean-burn engine cut soot about a thousandfold, but tinier exhaust particles that can seed contrails stayed about the same.

ByLuis Arrais
Author
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 6:58
Instaread
Follow Earth on Google

Those white streaks behind a jet look like pure cloud, but in most of today’s jet engines, the ice in them forms mainly on specks of soot.

One newer engine design, run the way it was built to run, leaves almost none of that soot behind.

Scientists flew a research jet through the exhaust of two Airbus airliners.

Behind engines running normally, they measured about a thousand times fewer soot particles than when the same engines were forced to burn a richer mix of fuel.

A second kind of particle, far smaller and formed from gases in the exhaust, stayed at about the same count. How many of those turned up depended on what was in the fuel tank, and even on which engine burned it.

Rebecca Dischl led the work at the German Aerospace Center’s Institute of Atmospheric Physics and Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz.

The team tested one engine type on two planes, so the results describe that engine rather than every jet in the sky.

Flying into another plane’s exhaust

The measuring plane was a small Falcon 20 jet carrying particle counters and gas sensors.

It trailed an Airbus A319neo in November 2021 and an A321neo in March 2023, flying oval loops in closed airspace off France’s Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts.

Both airliners flew on LEAP-1A engines. Engineers from Airbus and Safran Aircraft Engines are among the co-authors.

Usually approaching from slightly below and to the right, the Falcon climbed into the plume about 100 to 820 feet (30 to 250 meters) behind the engine. At that distance, the exhaust was between a tenth of a second and 1.4 seconds old.

The flights stayed in warm, dry air where no contrail could form, so the instruments caught raw exhaust.

A Falcon can’t fly as fast as an airliner cruises, so the airliners slowed down to match. The team estimated that the slower speed changed soot output by less than 5%.

Lean burning cut the soot

Inside a lean-burn engine, fuel and air are mixed before they ignite, which gives a more even flame with fewer fuel-rich pockets. Those pockets are where soot forms.

These engines normally switch to a richer mode only for moments like startup, quick throttle changes or low power.

For the tests, the engine’s computer was set to hold that richer mode at cruise settings so the two could be compared directly.

Running lean, the engines put out about a thousand times fewer soot particles than in the forced rich mode.

That count came close to the ordinary background of particles in the air, and below the lowest values that contrail computer models often assume.

Yet the total number of particles, soot plus the smaller kind, stayed in about the same range in both modes. Burning lean got rid of the soot but not most of the other particles.

Cleaner fuel cut both kinds

The team also switched fuels. The standard was ordinary jet fuel from the airport in Toulouse.

The alternative was a sustainable fuel made by treating fats and oils with hydrogen. Some batches had added ring-shaped molecules called aromatics, which ordinary jet fuel also contains.

In the rich mode, pure sustainable fuel cut soot particles by 64% compared with ordinary fuel. In lean mode, it cut them by 25%. Soot dropped off sharply as a fuel’s hydrogen content rose.

Aromatics had the opposite effect. They carry less hydrogen, and the blend with the most added aromatics made about as much soot as ordinary fuel.

Sulfur mattered for the smaller particles. Nearly sulfur-free fuels cut them by up to 80%, while ordinary jet fuel typically holds 200 to 400 parts per million of sulfur.

Even the Toulouse fuel was cleaner than the world average. Against typical fuel, engine models suggest the soot cuts could be larger.

Two matching engines behaved differently

On one flight, the Falcon sampled the left and right engines of the A321neo back to back. Both burned the same ordinary fuel at similar power.

Soot came out about the same from each. But the left engine put out about ten times more of the smaller particles.

That engine was more worn, with a deterioration rating of 50%, versus 30% for the right engine. The rating reflects lost performance relative to a new engine.

It also used about 20% more oil, though that amount remained within normal limits.

In this engine, some oil is vented into the hot exhaust, where it could form extra small particles. Ordinary differences between individual engines may also explain part of the gap.

A cockpit photo taken on a different day showed a thinner contrail behind the right engine than the left. Those smaller particles aren’t part of engine certification tests, so for most engines their numbers are largely unknown.

Small particles now matter more

Once soot is scarce, the smaller particles likely become an important seed for the ice in contrails. Contrails may warm the planet as much as aviation’s carbon dioxide does, or more, though the uncertainty is large.

Another team has estimated that avoiding contrails by changing altitude could cut aviation’s warming quickly.

Tiny exhaust particles matter at ground level too.

Other researchers have measured large spikes of them near airports, and the authors wrote that cleaner fuels and engines may improve air quality there.

Cutting sulfur comes with a trade-off the authors flag. Sulfur particles reflect some sunlight and make low clouds brighter, both of which cool the planet.

Today’s jet fuel can contain up to half of this kind of sustainable fuel, and a standard for using it pure is in development.

Most of the test fuels wouldn’t meet current rules, because aromatics help keep seals in aircraft fuel systems working. Making enough of it is its own problem, with U.S. supply projected to fall short of its 2030 target.

What remains unknown

Every measurement here was taken within about a second and a half of the exhaust leaving the engine.

Smaller particles keep growing for minutes, so the two burning modes might look different farther back in the plume.

The forced rich mode also isn’t identical to the most common engines flying today, which start their burn rich by design.

How other engines, fuels and levels of wear change particle counts remains an open question.

The authors call for measurements across a wider range of engines and fuels. They also want direct tests of how the smaller particles turn into contrail ice.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.
